claims.text: An audit log records who did what to which resource, when and with what outcome, kept as later evidence (glossary definition; outline item 1).
A cryptographic hash changes when any input byte changes; an entry's hash computed over its fields and prev_hash links it to the entry before.
Tamper-evident means a change leaves a mark a check can find: a hash chain shows any changed entry, and any removed entry that has entries after it; it makes tampering visible, not impossible.

Changing one entry makes its recomputed hash and every later one differ from the stored ones; removing an entry with entries after it breaks the link at the next entry (its prev_hash no longer matches); removing the newest entries leaves a shorter chain that still checks.
claims.source_hint: docs/design/audit-log.md lines 42-47 @ stage-4; follows from claim 5 (each hash covers prev_hash)

claims.text: The design's verify job recomputes the chain periodically and reports the first place it is wrong.
A chain alone does not stop someone who can rewrite an entry and every later entry (recomputing their hashes), nor removal of the newest entries; the append-only store is what limits who can try.
claims.source_hint: follows from claim 7; audit-log.md lines 49-54 @ stage-4 (store design)

claims.text: Entries go to a store separate from the services' databases where services may only append (no change, no delete); donhang and any database user a service connects as have no rights on it; only auditors and the team lead read it; product not chosen.
A transparency log, where Cosign records signing events (Rekor), is a record that is kept, not rewritten, so a later change can be noticed.
claims.source_hint: Sigstore Cosign docs, Signing overview: Rekor, a signature transparency log, immutable; devops.l3.signing-images summary line 3

claims.text: RecordOrderStatusHistory writes Order, Event, Status and OccurredAt to order_status_history; no field names who acted.

audit-log.md audits: ship (PATCH /api/v1/orders/{id}/ship, API), refund request (POST /api/v1/orders/{id}/refund, API), product price change (PATCH /api/v1/products/{id}, API), Keycloak role grant/removal (Keycloak; how decided later), invoice signing request (Payments).

Entry fields: actor (sub from the checked token; a background job writes the service name), action, resource, at, outcome (allowed/denied/failed with error code), prev_hash, hash; no token, password, key or secret in any entry, even when the action failed because of one.
At stage-4 the audit log is a plan only: audit-log.md says not built; threat-model.md defers P4 to it.

Trade-offs: own-table columns and Loki lines cost nothing extra but can be changed or written unseen by the services; a separate hash-chained append-only store shows who acted for listed actions at the cost of a store, a verify job, per-action entries and a retention decision.
backend-review-checklist.md asks of every new action whether it must be recorded in the audit log (audit-log.md).
Debugging overnight refund failures belongs to Loki and traces; the audit log says who asked and whether it was allowed, not what broke.
The Authorization header of a request to the API carries the caller's access token (Bearer), so recording whole requests would put tokens into entries.
claims.source_hint: RFC 6750 section 2.1 (Authorization Request Header Field); backend.l4.signing-key-custody claim 2 (Bearer header in Đơn Hàng)

claims.text: Append-only permissions bind the services, not whoever administers the store, and do not stop a service from appending a false entry; the chain shows later changes, not whether an entry was true.
An audit log records the actions someone may later need to prove (those audit-log.md lists), not every request; recording every request buries them among reads and carries tokens.
The sub field of an access token (JWT) names the signed-in user; the design's actor is that sub taken from the checked token.
claims.source_hint: RFC 7519 section 4.1.2 (sub, Subject claim); docs/design/audit-log.md line 33 @ stage-4
